newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Buyoya still unsure of seat at Burundi summit.
newsitem.headline: Buyoya still unsure of seat at Burundi summit.

text.p: Burundi's military leader made clear on Thursday regional leaders had still not invited him to next weekend's summit on the worsening crisis in his country.
Major Pierre Buyoya told reporters in Bujumbura he would only agree to attend the summit as head of state, not merely as the army's representative.

He said the international mediator for Burundi, former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, assured him on Wednesday Hutu rebel leaders would not take part in the summit due to be held in Arusha, Tanzania.
"President Nyerere again promised to convince heads of state to invite Burundi. We await their reaction," Buyoya said.
"There is no suggestion of inviting faction leaders, I received assurances on that point," he told a news conference.
All Burundi's neighbours as well as Kenya clamped a total trade and transport embargo on Burundi last July 31 as a penalty for the coup by the mainly-Tutsi army six days earlier.
The key condition for easing or lifting sanctions are that Buyoya agrees unconditional talks with Hutu rebels and their main leader, Leonard Nyangoma.

Most embassies in Bujumbura fear that if Buyoya is forced into talks with Nyangoma and sanctions are not lifted, his reign may end abruptly and be replaced by hardliners bent on a solely military approach to the rebels.
Buyoya said he wanted to go to the Arusha summit to explain his peace plan and the "perverse and devastating" effects of sanctions.
"We have asked to be invited as head of state of Burundi," he said in reply to suggestions the leaders might invite him as army representative.
"It is clear I will not go unless it is as head of state."
Buyoya made a day trip to see Nyerere in Musoma, Tanzania, on Wednesday.
"The embargo is part of the war being waged against Burundi on several levels. The Burundian people have to be prepared to fight this war on all levels," he said on Thursday.

The sanctions are preventing exports of coffee and tea, government officials say. But observers in the capital and visitors to border regions say imports of fuel and basic commodities are crossing the porous borders with Rwanda, Tanzania and Zaire.
